title: Emotions and the Immune System
text: Can our emotional states influence our physical biology and immune function? Peer-reviewed clinical research has shown that negative emotional states—such as chronic depressive symptoms—are linked to dysregulated immune responses and chronic low-grade systemic inflammation (e.g., Wang et al., 2023, Journal of Affective Disorders).

About the Dataset
This analysis uses publicly available data from the CDC National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES):

Observations: 4,864 adult respondents (exceeding the 1,000 observation minimum).
Key Variables: 10 measurements including respondent ID (SEQN), age, gender, depression screener score (phq9_score), clinical severity category (depression_level), white blood cell count (wbc_count), neutrophil count (neutrophils), lymphocyte count (lymphocytes), platelet count (platelets), and systemic immune-inflammation index (sii).
Data Source: Reliable, open-access public health surveillance from the CDC.
Dataset URL: CDC NHANES 2017–2018 Data Portal.

title: Emotions and the Immune System
section: Visualizing Immune Inflammation Across Depression Levels
text:
Visualizing Immune Inflammation Across Depression Levels
The Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII) is calculated as: \[\text{SII} = \frac{\text{Platelets} \times \text{Neutrophils}}{\text{Lymphocytes}}\]
Elevated SII scores reflect heightened immune inflammation. Below, we compare median SII values across categories of depressive symptom severity assessed by the PHQ-9.





Median Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII) by depression severity category.

title: Emotions and the Immune System
text:
Key Takeaway
As depression severity increases from “None” to “Severe”, median SII rises from 428.2 to 475.0, illustrating the biological link between emotional distress and systemic immune activation documented in peer-reviewed literature.
